title: Continuous batching scheduler — tuning experiments (batch size, timeout, fairness, tail latency)
content:
Overview:
We ran a set of controlled experiments to understand how continuous-batching scheduler knobs impact user-visible latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput, and fairness across heterogeneous request sizes. This is an iterative follow-on to previous notes (see linked artifacts) — primary goal is to pick a safe default config and a canary rollout plan for Dedicated and Hosted.

Goals:
- Measure the trade-off surface between batch size, timeout (max_wait_ms), and tail latency (p99/p999).
- Evaluate fairness policies that prevent starvation of small/interactive requests when batching favors large examples.
- Provide recommended defaults and a short rollout playbook (canary, metrics, rollback).

Experiment setup:
- Code branch: perf/scheduler-experiments (PR #412).
- Cluster: staging-dedicated-8xA100 (8 machines, mixed T4/40GB A100 in separate node pools).
- Runtime: serving-runtime v3.4.1 + continuous-batching scheduler module toggled.
- Models: rw-open-30b (dense) and rw-llm-7b (small) via model variants to test sequence-length sensitivity.
- Traffic generator: trace-replay of production sampling (3 customer traces) + synthetic poisson traffic to stress edge cases.
- Metrics: request latency histograms (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999), effective_batch_size distribution, GPU utilization, queue length, throughput (req/s), and fairness index (Jain's index across request size bins).

Knobs under test:
- max_batch_size (16, 32, 64, 128)
- max_wait_ms / timeout (2ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms)
- fairness_mode (none, size-weighted, priority-queues)
- min_batch_fill (0.25..1.0 expressed as fraction of max_batch_size)
- tail_latency_target_ms (soft target used by adaptive timeout controller: 50ms, 75ms, 100ms)

Workloads:
- Interactive small requests: avg tokens=40, latency-sensitive.
- Mixed webhook workloads: avg tokens=160, variable arrival.
- Batch/analytics style: avg tokens=800, throughput-oriented.
- Combined runs include 70% interactive, 20% mixed, 10% batch to match product mix.

Key results (high-level):
1) Batch size vs latency:
   - Increasing max_batch_size from 32->128 improved throughput by ~18% for large-model runs, but p99 tail latency increased substantially for interactive requests unless max_wait_ms is tightened.
   - Effective batch_size distribution: with max_batch_size=128 and default timeout=10ms, median effective batch=48, long tail of ~120 (when bursty traffic).

2) Timeout (max_wait_ms):
   - Lowering timeout from 10ms->2ms reduced p95/p99 for interactive class by ~20-35% at cost of 6-10% throughput loss.
   - 5ms provided a reasonable balance in most mixed workloads; 2ms is only viable when strict p99 SLOs exist.

3) Fairness policies:
   - size-weighted fairness (small requests prioritized by lowering their effective wait) improved p99 for interactive group by ~40% vs no fairness, with only ~3% throughput regression.
   - Priority-queues (hard priority for small requests) eliminated most small-request tail but caused starvation for large-batch throughput in sustained load — not acceptable for Dedicated where customers expect throughput SLAs.

4) Adaptive timeout with tail_latency_target:
   - Adaptive controller that reduces timeout when p99 exceeds tail_latency_target_ms stabilized tails across bursts. Setting target=75ms reduced p99 spikes by ~30% compared to fixed 10ms timeout in bursty traces.
   - Controller oscillation observed when aggressive target used (50ms) — requires hysteresis and smoothing.

Detailed observations and notes:
- GPU utilization correlates strongly with effective_batch_size; aggressive batching improves hardware efficiency but can degrade interactive p99 unless fairness or tight timeouts are applied.
- For rw-llm-7b (shorter kernel times), batching is less beneficial; small timeouts are enough to keep throughput high while maintaining low tail latency. For rw-open-30b, batching gains are larger.
- Jain's fairness index improved from 0.62 -> 0.88 with size-weighted fairness; priority-queues pushed index >0.95 but harmed throughput.
- In flight-request jitter tests (spiky arrival), fixed timeout leads to transient p99 spikes; adaptive timeout smooths but needs dampening parameters (alpha=0.2, window=5s found reasonable).

Recommended defaults (for Hosted and Dedicated conservative baseline):
- max_batch_size: 64
- max_wait_ms: 5ms
- fairness_mode: size-weighted
- min_batch_fill: 0.5
- adaptive_tail_target_ms: 75ms with smoothing alpha=0.2, min_timeout=2ms, max_timeout=25ms
Rationale: Balanced throughput improvements for medium/large models while keeping interactive p99 within acceptable bounds.

Canary rollout plan:
1) Deploy config to a single dedicated node pool (10% of capacity) for 24 hours.
2) Monitor the following dashboards/alerts: p99_interactive > 90ms, effective_batch_size median deviation >20% vs baseline, throughput degradation >8%, Jain fairness index <0.7.
3) If alerts fire, roll back to previous scheduler config and open an incident.
4) If stable for 48h, expand to 50% capacity; full rollout after 7 days of stable metrics.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How does the scheduler interact with KV-cache eviction under large batches? Need a follow-up test that tracks KV cache hit-rate vs batch size.
- Add more production traces from APAC region (we only used NA/EU samples).
- Explore hybrid fairness: size-weighted with occasional strict small-request windows during high percentile spikes.
- Tune adaptive controller hysteresis to avoid oscillation under periodic traffic patterns.

Appendix — raw numbers (selected):
- Mixed trace (70/20/10) / rw-open-30b:
  - max_batch_size=64, timeout=5ms, fairness=size-weighted -> p50=18ms, p95=42ms, p99=86ms, throughput=12.8 req/s/node, GPU util=78%
  - max_batch_size=128, timeout=10ms, fairness=none -> p50=20ms, p95=54ms, p99=160ms, throughput=15.1 req/s/node, GPU util=89%
  - max_batch_size=32, timeout=2ms, fairness=size-weighted -> p50=16ms, p95=36ms, p99=74ms, throughput=11.9 req/s/node, GPU util=71%

- Adaptive controller (target=75ms) reduced p99 spikes by ~30% compared to fixed 10ms timeout across bursty traces.

Contacts / next steps:
- Engineering leads: Ethan Park (owner), Priya Singh (scheduler impl), Marco Alvarez (bench harness).
- Follow-up ticket: JIRA ENGINF-821 (adaptive controller hysteresis + KV-cache test).
- PR to merge config defaults: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412

Notes to self / rough ideas (informal):
- Consider exposing a per-customer policy API for Dedicated customers to tune fairness vs throughput (but default must be conservative).
- Could experiment with neural schedulers (learning-based timeouts) but that's 2-3 quarters out.
- Add unit tests for fairness mode to ensure no regression when we change batching heuristics.
